extracted.intended_audience: researchers, university/industry applicants, and the general public seeking information about AFRL/AFOSR organization and funding priorities
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) and the Air Force Office of Scientific Research (AFOSR), including organizational structure, directorate missions, research/funding emphases, and example programs that indicate what types of research are prioritized and funded.

rubrics_metrics.name: AFOSR funding mission
rubrics_metrics.description: The Air Force Office of Scientific Research (AFOSR) invests in basic research efforts for the Air Force by funding investigation in relevant scientific areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AFOSR's research is organized into four scientific directorates (Engineering and Complex Systems; Information and Networks; Physical Sciences; Chemistry and Biological Sciences). AFOSR funds activities it believes will enable the technological superiority of the Air Force, maintains foreign technology offices (London, Tokyo, Santiago) to coordinate international collaboration, and sponsors programs such as the University Nanosatellite Program.

rubrics_metrics.name: AFRL headquarters responsibilities / priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: AFRL Headquarters is responsible for leadership, policy and guidance; unifying objectives of technical directorates, the 711th wing, and AFOSR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headquarters staff functions include Public Relations, Strategic Communication, Business Outreach, Planning, Programming, Budgeting and Execution (PPBE), Technology Transition, Transformation, Contracting and a High-Performance Computing Center. HQ also includes the Center for Rapid Innovation, which handles urgent operational requests from commanders (e.g., Air Force Space Command, Global Strike Command, Air Mobility Command).

rubrics_metrics.name: AFRL organizational model: directorates vs AFOSR
rubrics_metrics.description: The laboratory is divided into eight Technical Directorates, one wing, and the Air Force Office of Scientific Research (AFOSR); AFOSR is primarily a funding body for external research while the other directorates perform research in-house or under contract to external entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A directorate is roughly equivalent to a military wing and is composed of divisions (research and support). Typical support divisions: Operations and Integration (business computing, HR, business development), Financial Management, Procurement. Understanding this split helps determine whether work should be proposed to AFOSR (external basic research funding) or to a directorate (internal/contract research).

rubrics_metrics.name: Air Vehicles Directorate mission / fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Mission: developing technologies that support cost-effective and survivable aerospace vehicles capable of accurate and quick delivery of a variety of future weapons or cargo anywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects and examples include lifting-body research (X-24), X-53 Active Aeroelastic Wing, collaborations with NASA and industry (Boeing), Advanced Composite Cargo Aircraft demonstrator, X-37/X-40 spacecraft work, and hypersonic/reusable booster initiatives. Proposals aligned to vehicle efficiency, survivability, novel airframe concepts, and vehicle demonstrations are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed Energy Directorate mission / fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Center of Excellence for high power microwave technology and the Department of Defense's Center of Expertise for laser development of all types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directed Energy projects typically fall into two categories: laser and microwave. Work spans non-lethal targeting lasers and dazzlers (PHaSR), high-energy chemical oxygen iodine lasers (COIL) for missile defense, and high-power microwave applications (including Active Denial System). Be aware of ethical, legal, and human-rights concerns raised in the public record (e.g., blindness concerns, Amnesty International/Human Rights Watch criticisms) when proposing human-directed effects research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center for Rapid Innovation (rapid operational requests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Center within AFRL HQ that handles urgent operational requests from commanders (e.g., Air Force Space Command, Air Force Global Strike Command, Air Mobility Command).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This center is oriented to rapid response and transition to operational needs; proposals or requests addressing urgent warfighter needs and rapid development/transition may be channeled here rather than through normal long-term basic research mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: 711th Human Performance Wing mission / fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Vision includes improving aerospace medicine, science and technology, and human systems integration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied work in human performance such as ejection system safety, anthropometry for diverse aircrew (whole-body scanning), human-systems integration, and aerospace medicine aligns with this wing's priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Directorate mission / fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead the discovery, development, and integration of affordable warfighting information technologies for air, space, and cyberspace forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past contributions include work on ARPANET-related technologies, Joint Surveillance Target Attack Radar System (JSTARS), and voice stress analysis. Proposals emphasizing affordable, deployable information systems, sensor-to-shooter integration, and communications/command-and-control technologies match this directorate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials and Manufacturing Directorate mission / fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Develops materials, processes, and advanced manufacturing technologies for aerospace systems and their components to improve Air Force capabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: development of rare-earth magnet materials, novel manufacturing methods for turbine exhaust casings (cost and durability improvements), laser-based ultrasonic inspection for composites, advanced thermoplastic composites, and fiber-optic fabric for friend-or-foe identification. Proposals improving material performance, manufacturability, inspection, and life-cycle cost are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Munitions Directorate mission / fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Mission: develop, demonstrate and transition science and technology for air-launched munitions for defeating ground fixed, mobile/relocatable, air and space targets to assure pre-eminence of U.S. air and space forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public examples: rapid concept-to-deployment munitions like the GBU-28 and large ordnance such as the GBU-43/B. Proposals should emphasize lethality, survivability, rapid development, transition pathways, and operational relevance for air-launched weapons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propulsion Directorate mission / fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Mission: create and transition propulsion and power technology for military dominance of air and space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research areas include experimental rocket propulsion, aircraft power systems (e.g., lithium-ion main aircraft battery), scramjet/hypersonic propulsion (X-51A), pulse detonation engines, and rocket engine testing (RS-68). Proposals concerning propulsion performance, power systems, and transition to flight test are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensors Directorate mission, core technology areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Mission: provide a full range of air and space sensors, networked to the warfighter, providing a complete and timely picture of the battlespace enabling precision targeting and protection of friendly assets. Core technology areas include radar, active and passive electro-optical targeting systems, navigation aids, automatic target recognition, sensor fusion, threat warning and countermeasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past technical achievements include contributions to DARPA/ISIS projects, transparent transistor demonstrations, and sensor fusion advances. Proposals addressing sensing modalities, multi-sensor fusion, autonomy in target recognition, and deployable sensor systems align with this directorate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space Vehicles Directorate mission / fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Mission: develop and transition space technologies for more effective, more affordable warfighter missions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities and examples: HAARP (ionospheric research), radiation-hardened flight computers (IBM RAD6000), nanosatellite programs (University Nanosatellite Program), TacSat responsive space efforts, and the Space University Research Initiative (SURI) which supports multidisciplinary basic and applied research to transition aerospace concepts such as on-orbit servicing, assembly, and manufacturing (OSAM). Proposals for satellite tech, deployable structures, space sensors, and affordable responsive space capabilities are applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: AFRL control of Air Force science & technology budget
rubrics_metrics.description: AFRL controls the entire Air Force science and technology research budget (noted as $2.4 billion in 2006).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AFRL's budget authority indicates centralized planning and priority-setting for Air Force S&T — alignment to AFRL/AFOSR priorities and mission areas increases the likelihood of funding. Understanding PPBE (Planning, Programming, Budgeting and Execution) processes at AFRL HQ can help align proposals with funded priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program-level initiatives (University Nanosatellite Program, SURI)
rubrics_metrics.description: AFRL/AFOSR sponsor programmatic initiatives such as the University Nanosatellite Program (a satellite design and fabrication competition) and the Space University Research Initiative (SURI) to foster engagement among DoD, academia, and industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These programs emphasize student/university participation, technology transition, multidisciplinary collaboration, and demonstrable flight or on-orbit capability. SURI explicitly supports projects (e.g., OSAM) that transition basic/applied research into advanced technologies with operational impact.
